title: Nuh and the Vanished Nations
question: Why does the Quran keep returning to nations that vanished?
summary: Follow Nuh through nine and a half centuries of calling and the Flood, then the ruined peoples of 'Ad, Thamud, Lut and Madyan, and see the single pattern the Quran draws from them all.

cover.alt: A great wooden ship riding mountainous waves under a dark sky, with a break of light in the clouds
cover.prompt: A great wooden ship of planks and pegs riding enormous dark waves like mountains under a storm-black sky, rain sheeting down, a single break in the clouds letting a shaft of pale light fall on the water ahead.

chapters.title: Nine and a Half Centuries of Asking

blocks.p: The Quran gives one number for Nuh's mission, and it is staggering: "he remained among them a thousand years minus fifty years" (29:14). Nine hundred and fifty years of the same message. Generations were born, grew old and died hearing it. Grandchildren heard it from the same man who had warned their grandparents.

The message itself was short: "Worship Allah, fear Him and obey me" (71:3). The answer from the people who mattered was always some version of the same contempt. "We do not see you but as a man like ourselves," said the eminent among them, "and we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us" (11:27). They wanted him to drive away his poor followers before they would listen. He refused: "I am not one to drive away those who have believed" (11:29).

Then came the word that no more of them would believe, and an instruction: "construct the ship under Our observation and Our inspiration" (11:37). Picture a ship being built far from any sea, plank by plank, for years. The Quran gives the scene a single, perfect sentence:

Surah al-Qamar adds the plainest detail of all. Allah carried him "on a [construction of] planks and nails" (54:13). No dimensions, no timber names, no count of decks. Those details exist in older traditions, but the Quran does not need them. What it records is a man building in obedience while the respectable people of his town walked past laughing, and a short sentence of his in reply: you will come to know.

Al-Qamar also records his shortest prayer, said after nearly a millennium of effort: "Indeed, I am overpowered, so help" (54:10). Three words in Arabic, *anni maghlubun fantasir*. It is not the prayer of a man who failed to try.

chapters.title: A Prophet Reports to His Lord

blocks.p: Surah Nuh, the seventy-first chapter, is unusual. Most of it is Nuh speaking to Allah, giving an account of his mission like a servant reporting back after a long assignment. Read the heart of it:

Every line shows a different method. "Night and day": he did not wait for convenient hours. "Publicly", then "announced... and confided to them secretly": crowds, open declaration, private conversation. Scholars of da'wah, the call to Islam, still point to these verses as a summary of how to invite people: try every door.

And every line shows a different refusal. They put their fingers in their ears. They "covered themselves with their garments", pulling their clothes over their heads so they would not have to see him. This is not a failure of argument. It is a decision not to hear.

Then look at what he offered. Not only threats. "Ask forgiveness of your Lord", and the promise that follows is concrete: rain in continuing showers, wealth, children, gardens and rivers. The word *istighfar*, seeking forgiveness, is tied here to the most worldly blessings a farming people could want. The next verses add an argument from creation: Allah made you "in stages" (71:14), raised the seven heavens and made "the moon therein a [reflected] light and made the sun a burning lamp" (71:16).

The surah ends with a prayer that every Muslim can say, and many do: "My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house a believer and the believing men and believing women" (71:28). After nine centuries of rejection, Nuh's last recorded words still include everyone who believes.

The sign came: "the oven overflowed" (11:40). Water began to burst from the ground where no water should be. Surah al-Qamar describes it from both directions at once: "We opened the gates of the heaven with rain pouring down and caused the earth to burst with springs, and the waters met" (54:11-12). Nuh loaded a pair of each creature, his family, and the few who believed, and blessed its voyage in words Muslims still say when they set out: *bismillahi majreha wa mursaha*, "in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage" (11:41).

blocks.alt: A wooden ship on enormous waves beside a dark mountain rising out of the flood
blocks.caption: "And it sailed with them through waves like mountains" (11:42).
blocks.prompt: Enormous grey-green waves rising like mountains in driving rain, a heavy wooden ship climbing one crest, and nearby the dark summit of a mountain still standing above the flood, under a low storm sky.

blocks.p: Then the most painful scene in the story.

Read the father's words again: *ya bunayya*, "O my little son", a tender diminutive, used for a grown man in mortal danger. The son's reply is the reply of every confident person who trusts the high ground of their own plans. And then, in four Arabic words, *wa hala baynahuma al-mawj*, the waves came between them.

Afterwards, when the earth had swallowed its water and the ship had come to rest on al-Judi, Nuh called to his Lord. He did not argue; he reminded: "my son is of my family; and indeed, Your promise is true" (11:45). The answer was hard. "He is not of your family; indeed, he is [one whose] work was other than righteous" (11:46). Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, insist he was truly Nuh's son; what cut him off from the family of salvation was his deeds, not his birth. Nuh accepted it at once, seeking refuge from asking what he did not know (11:47).

The Quran lets the lesson stand without comment. A prophet's son drowned. A prophet's wife, it says elsewhere, was among the lost (66:10). Faith is not inherited, and it cannot be carried on someone else's back.

chapters.title: Wadd, Suwa', and the First Statues

blocks.p: Surah Nuh names five idols that the leaders told the people never to abandon: "Wadd or Suwa' or Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr" (71:23). Where did they come from? Al-Bukhari preserves an answer from Ibn 'Abbas, the Prophet's ﷺ cousin and the foremost early interpreter of the Quran.

These, he said, were the names of righteous men among Nuh's people. When they died, Satan suggested to their community that they set up images in their gathering places and call them by their names, so that their memory would inspire people. That generation did not worship them. But when they passed away and knowledge faded, the next generations did. Ibn 'Abbas added that the same names later turned up as idols among Arab tribes.

The account is quietly devastating. Idolatry, in this telling, did not begin with wickedness. It began with love for good people and a wish to remember them, and slid, over generations, into worship. Scholars cite it as the reason Islam is so watchful about venerating graves and images: the road to shirk, associating others with Allah, can start with good intentions.

blocks.note: Classical commentators mostly held that the Flood covered the whole earth, citing Nuh's prayer "do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant" (71:26) and the verse "We made his descendants those remaining" (37:77). Some modern Muslim scholars argue it was regional, covering the whole of Nuh's people and their land, noting that *ard* can mean "land" as well as "earth" and that Nuh was sent to his own people only. The Quran's moral point is the same on either reading.
blocks.title: Where scholars differ: how wide was the Flood?

blocks.p: The commentaries also contain many details the Quran does not: the son's name (Kan'an), the number aboard (eighty, or fewer), the ship's length in cubits, the date it sailed. Al-Jalalayn and others pass these on with phrases like "according to the story" and "it is said". Many come from *Isra'iliyyat*, Jewish and Christian lore, or from unverified early reports. They may be true or not; Muslims are not required to believe them. The same goes for the oven: Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have taken *tannur* as the face of the earth, while others took it as a real baking oven.
Surah ash-Shu'ara, "The Poets", tells the stories of Nuh and four later messengers one after another, and opens each with nearly identical words. Here is Nuh:

Now Hud, sent to 'Ad: "'Aad denied the messengers, when their brother Hud said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah? Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger...'" (26:123-127). Then Salih to Thamud (26:141-145), Lut to his people (26:160-164), and Shu'ayb (26:176-180). The repetition is the point. The surah is showing that the messengers were not five religions but one voice, speaking to five different peoples.
Note too what each says: "they denied the messengers", plural, though each people rejected one man. To reject one messenger is to reject them all, because they carry the same message.

word.nuance: The messengers are called "their brother": Nuh, Hud, Salih and Lut were from their people, spoke their language and knew their lives. Strikingly, Shu'ayb is not called "brother" of the people of the thicket (26:177), though he is "their brother" to Madyan (11:84). Ibn Kathir explains that the people of the thicket were named after a tree they worshipped; al-Jalalayn says he was not of their lineage.

blocks.p: After the shared opening, each story turns to that nation's particular wrong. The message is one; the diseases differ.

right.title: The wrong named
items: Monuments and fortresses built in tyranny (26:128-130)
Indecency no one had done before (7:80)

blocks.p: The Quran's first listeners did not have to imagine these nations. They had passed their remains. "Indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night. Then will you not use reason?" (37:137-138). The Makkan caravans ran north to Syria along routes lined with ruins.

'Ad lived in the south, in al-Ahqaf, the region of curving sand dunes (46:21). The Quran calls them "Iram, who had lofty pillars, the likes of whom had never been created in the land" (89:7-8), a people who asked, "Who is greater than us in strength?" (41:15). A screaming wind came "for seven nights and eight days", leaving them "as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees" (69:7).

Thamud lived in the north, in al-Hijr, "who carved out the rocks in the valley" (89:9). They were given a living sign: a she-camel, with a rule to share the water with her on alternate days (26:155). They hamstrung her. Salih gave them three days (11:65), and then "the shriek seized them at early morning" (15:83).

blocks.alt: Tall tomb facades carved into sandstone outcrops in a desert valley at dusk
blocks.caption: "They used to carve from the mountains, houses, feeling secure" (15:82).
blocks.prompt: Massive sandstone outcrops in a silent desert valley at dusk, tall doorways and facades carved into the rock, long shadows, an old stone well in the foreground and an empty caravan track running past.

blocks.p: In the year 9 AH (630 CE), the Prophet ﷺ led an army north to Tabuk and passed through al-Hijr. Al-Bukhari and Muslim report what he did there. He told his companions not to enter the dwellings of those who had wronged themselves except weeping, lest what struck them strike you. Then he covered his head with his cloak and hurried his mount until he had crossed the valley. When some companions drew water from Thamud's wells and made dough with it, he told them to pour the water out and feed the dough to the camels, and to draw instead from the well the she-camel had drunk from.
Those sandstone tombs still stand in north-western Arabia. Visitors photograph them. The Prophet ﷺ taught his companions to pass them with tears.

A thoughtful reader may be uneasy. Floods, winds, earthquakes: are these stories teaching that natural disasters are Allah's anger? If so, what of the children who drown, the believers caught in the same earthquake? And what of today, when some preachers announce that a hurricane was punishment for someone's sins?

The Quran sets strict conditions around these destructions. First, none came without a messenger and a long warning: "never would We punish until We sent a messenger" (17:15). Second, none came while people were striving to do right: "your Lord would not have destroyed the cities unjustly while their people were reformers" (11:117). Third, the believers were saved each time, and the outcome followed sustained, informed refusal. "Allah would not have wronged them, but it was they who were wronging themselves" (29:40).

Those conditions cannot be checked from outside for any modern event. There is no prophet among us whose warning a city has just rejected. That is why careful scholars refuse to declare that any particular disaster is a punishment. The hadith goes the other way: the Prophet ﷺ said, as al-Bukhari reports, that a believer who dies of plague or drowning or under a collapsed building dies a martyr. Suffering, for a believer, can be a raising of rank, not a sentence.

So what are the stories for? The Quran calls the pattern *sunnat Allah*, "the way of Allah", and says it never changes (35:43). Its point is moral, not meteorological: arrogance, injustice and contempt for truth destroy communities, and people are given time to turn back. The Quran presents itself as that warning, delivered before the end rather than after it.

Muslims believe the destructions were real events. A sceptic may doubt them. But the argument of the stories does not depend on archaeology. It asks something every reader can test: have you seen proud power that refused all correction end any other way?

chapters.title: The Fingers in Our Own Ears

blocks.p: It is easy to read these chapters as stories about other people: the stubborn, the cruel, the cheats. The Quran does not let us. "Each [story] We relate to you from the news of the messengers is that by which We make firm your heart" (11:120). They were told first to strengthen the Prophet ﷺ, rejected in Makkah, and then to every reader after him.

So turn the questions inward. What truth have I heard many times and put my fingers in my ears against? What correction have I refused because it came from someone "lower" than me? What wealth or skill do I treat as proof that I am safe? 'Ad asked, "Who is greater than us in strength?" The question still gets asked, in every age.

And there is comfort for anyone who has tried for years to reach someone they love and failed. Nuh called his son from the deck of a ship. He was a prophet, and his plea for him was answered with a no. If you have done your part with sincerity, the outcome was never in your hands. You will be asked about your effort, not about another soul's choice.

Notice, too, that Nuh's grief did not turn into bitterness against Allah. He asked, he was corrected, and he said at once, "unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers" (11:47). Sorrow and surrender sat in the same sentence. That is the shape of a believer's heart in loss.
When Nuh's ship was built, he was told what to say on boarding and what to ask for at the end. Many Muslims recite his prayer when they arrive somewhere new:

chapters.title: Ask Forgiveness, and the Rain Will Come

blocks.p: The most practical line in today's reading is Nuh's offer: "Ask forgiveness of your Lord... He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in [continuing] showers" (71:10-11). Muslims have taken it seriously for fourteen centuries.

list: *Istighfar*, saying *astaghfirullah*, "I seek Allah's forgiveness", is part of daily life. The Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith in al-Bukhari, that he sought Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day.
When drought comes, Muslims hold *salat al-istisqa'*, the prayer for rain, which centres on seeking forgiveness. The Prophet ﷺ led it in Madinah.
Al-Qurtubi relates that men came to al-Hasan al-Basri with drought, poverty and a wish for children; he told each to seek forgiveness, and recited these verses.
Muslim traders take Shu'ayb's warning against short measure as business ethics: honest scales, honest invoices.

blocks.p: For a non-Muslim colleague or neighbour, this explains a habit you may have noticed: the murmured *astaghfirullah* after a mistake, a harsh word or a piece of bad news. It is not superstition. It is the reflex Nuh taught his people, and they refused: when something goes wrong, turn first to the One who forgives.

The stories also leave a quieter practice: travelling with open eyes. "Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them?" (30:9). When Muslims visit ancient ruins, many recall the Prophet's ﷺ manner at al-Hijr and treat the place as a lesson rather than a backdrop.
Try it today. Before sleep, say *astaghfirullah* slowly a hundred times, or simply once with full attention, and name to yourself one thing you are asking forgiveness for.

quiz.q: In 71:5-9, what do Nuh's methods of calling his people show?
options: That he gave up after a few attempts
That he tried every approach, night and day, publicly and privately
That he relied only on miracles
That he spoke only to the leaders
quiz.why: He called them "night and day" (71:5), "publicly" (71:8), and "announced to them and confided to them secretly" (71:9). The failure was their refusal, not his effort.

quiz.q: Why was Nuh's son not saved, according to 11:46?
options: He was not really Nuh's son
His deeds were not righteous, and kinship does not save
There was no room on the ship
quiz.why: 11:46: "he is not of your family; indeed, he is [one whose] work was other than righteous." Most commentators say he was truly Nuh's son; faith, not blood, decided.

quiz.q: What does the repeated opening in ash-Shu'ara (26:106-109, 26:124-127 and others) show?
options: That the stories were copied from each other
That each messenger brought a different religion
That the messengers brought one message to many peoples
That all five nations lived in the same city
quiz.why: Each says, "Will you not fear Allah? Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger... I do not ask you for it any payment." One message, many nations; only the specific wrong changes.

quiz.q: According to 11:117 and 17:15, when does Allah not destroy a community?
options: While its people are reformers, and before a messenger has warned them
Only if it has no idols
Whenever a prophet asks Him to spare it
quiz.why: 11:117: not "while their people were reformers". 17:15: "never would We punish until We sent a messenger." Warning and the chance to change always come first.

reflect: Nuh kept calling for centuries, and his son still refused. Is there someone you have stopped hoping for, or a truth you have stopped listening to? Write what one honest step toward either would look like.
